The `date` command printed "Sat Oct 3 03:48:16 PM EDT 2026", which tells us that it is currently Saturday, October 3rd, 2026 at 3:48:16 PM in Eastern Daylight Time. The output follows the standard Unix `date` format: abbreviated weekday, abbreviated month, day of month, time in hours:minutes:seconds with AM/PM, the timezone abbreviation (EDT, which is UTC-4 during daylight saving time), and the full four-digit year. Notice how the command picks up the system's timezone setting rather than assuming UTC, which is why we see EDT instead of something like "19:48:16 UTC".

Clocks on servers drift for several interconnected reasons, the most fundamental being that no real oscillator is perfectly stable — even high-quality quartz crystals used in server motherboards have small frequency errors on the order of a few parts per million, which accumulate into noticeable skew over days or weeks. Temperature changes inside a data center can shift the crystal's resonant frequency (a phenomenon known as temperature compensation error), while mechanical stresses, aging, and power-supply noise further degrade accuracy, and virtualization layers add their own timing jitter because the host kernel and hypervisor share a single physical clock among many virtual machines. To prevent cumulative drift from corrupting logs, certificate validation, database timestamps, and distributed-system coordination, servers synchronize to authoritative time sources using protocols like NTP (Network Time Protocol) or PTP (Precision Time Protocol), which continuously adjust the system clock toward a reference such as a GPS-disciplined oscillator or an atomic clock, keeping the drift bounded to milliseconds rather than letting it grow unbounded.
